title: Reading Rock Layers
description: The principles geologists use to interpret stacked strata

concepts.title: The Principle of Superposition
concepts.contentHtml:
The foundational rule of stratigraphy was articulated by Nicolaus Steno in 1669: in any undisturbed sequence of rock layers (strata), the oldest layers are at the bottom and the youngest are at the top.

This seems obvious, but it was a revolutionary insight — it meant you could read time directly from rock. Before Steno, there was no systematic way to determine which rocks were older. His principle works because sediments are deposited on top of earlier layers and lithify (turn to rock) below younger ones.

The principle holds unless the strata have been tilted, folded, or overturned by tectonic forces — which geologists must check for.

concepts.title: Original Horizontality and Lateral Continuity
concepts.contentHtml:
Two companion principles from Steno:

Original Horizontality: sediment layers are deposited horizontally. If you see tilted or folded strata, they were deformed after deposition. The angle of tilt tells you something happened — a tectonic event, compaction, or an ancient slope.

Lateral Continuity: strata extend laterally in all directions until they thin out at their edges or are cut off by another feature. A layer of limestone that appears in two cliff faces on opposite sides of a valley was originally one continuous sheet before the river carved through it.

concepts.title: Cross-Cutting Relationships
concepts.contentHtml:
Any geological feature (a fault, an igneous intrusion, an erosion surface) that cuts across existing rock layers must be younger than the layers it cuts. This is the principle of cross-cutting relationships.

For example, if a granite intrusion cuts through limestone beds, the granite is younger than the limestone. If a fault offsets a dyke, the fault is younger than the dyke.

Together with superposition and index fossils, cross-cutting relationships allow geologists to build a complete relative time sequence — the order of geological events — even without absolute dates.

title: Sedimentation and Rock Types
description: How sediment becomes rock and what it records

concepts.title: Sedimentary Environments
concepts.contentHtml:
Sedimentary rocks form wherever particles settle and accumulate. Each environment produces a distinctive rock type:

  • Rivers — coarse conglomerates and sandstones; cross-bedding indicates current direction.
  • Desert dunes — well-sorted sandstone with large-scale cross-bedding (e.g. Navajo Sandstone, USA).
  • Shallow marine shelf — limestones, shales; often rich in marine fossils.
  • Deep ocean — fine muds and oozes of silica or carbonate from settling plankton shells.
  • Swamps — organic-rich black shales and eventually coal (compressed plant matter).

concepts.title: Lithification — Turning Sediment to Stone
concepts.contentHtml:
Loose sediment becomes solid rock through two main processes:

Compaction — the weight of overlying sediment squeezes out water and pore space, pressing grains together. Shale (from mud) is almost entirely a product of compaction.

Cementation — mineral-rich groundwater circulates through pore spaces and deposits crystals of calcite, silica, or iron oxide that glue grains together. Sandstone gets its strength from cement between the grains.

Together, compaction and cementation constitute diagenesis — all the physical and chemical changes that transform sediment into sedimentary rock after burial.

concepts.title: Graded Bedding and Event Layers
concepts.contentHtml:
Graded bedding occurs when a single depositional event (a submarine landslide called a turbidity current, or a flood) dumps mixed sediment that settles out by size — coarse grains first, then finer. The result is a layer that grades from coarse at the base to fine at the top.

Geologists use graded bedding as a 'way-up' indicator: the coarse base confirms which side was originally down — critical when strata have been overturned by tectonics.

Single catastrophic events also leave distinctive event layers: the global iridium-rich clay layer at the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary marks the asteroid impact 66 million years ago and is found in outcrops on every continent.

title: The Geological Time Scale
description: How billions of years of Earth history are divided and named

concepts.title: Relative vs Absolute Time
concepts.contentHtml:
Stratigraphy originally dealt only with relative time — event A happened before event B — without knowing actual ages in years.

The geological time scale was built up through the 19th century by correlating rock sequences across Europe using index fossils. Geologists could say the Jurassic came before the Cretaceous decades before they had any idea both were tens of millions of years long.

Absolute time (radiometric dating) was added after the discovery of radioactivity in the early 20th century. Today the time scale is calibrated to millions of years, but the fundamental order was established purely from rock sequences and fossils.

concepts.title: Eons, Eras, Periods, and Epochs
concepts.contentHtml:
The geological time scale has a nested hierarchy:

  • Eon — largest unit. The Phanerozoic (541 Ma–present) covers visible life. Before that, the Precambrian covers 88 % of Earth's history.
  • Era — e.g. Paleozoic (ancient life), Mesozoic (middle life), Cenozoic (recent life).
  • Period — e.g. Jurassic, Cretaceous, Devonian.
  • Epoch — e.g. Pleistocene (ice ages), Holocene (present interglacial).

Boundaries between units are defined by major events — usually mass extinctions or rapid evolutionary radiations — visible in the global rock record.

concepts.title: Index Fossils — Biostratigraphy
concepts.contentHtml:
An index fossil belongs to a species that was geographically widespread but lived for only a short geological interval. When you find it in a rock, you know the rock is approximately that age.

Classic index fossils include:
— Ammonites: diverse, rapidly evolving, found globally in Mesozoic marine rocks.
— Trilobites: excellent Paleozoic index fossils.
— Foraminifera: single-celled organisms whose shells are used to date deep-sea cores to within tens of thousands of years.

Biostratigraphy — dating rocks using fossils — was the primary tool of the petroleum industry in the 20th century and remains critical today.

title: Famous Stratigraphic Sections
description: Rock outcrops that changed our understanding of deep time

concepts.title: The Grand Canyon — A Mile of Time
concepts.contentHtml:
The Grand Canyon in Arizona exposes nearly 2 billion years of Earth history in its walls — one of the most complete and accessible stratigraphic sections on Earth.

The Great Unconformity at its base is one of geology's most striking features: Cambrian sandstone (~525 Ma) sits directly on Precambrian granite (~1.7 Ga), with nearly 1.2 billion years of missing rock. This gap represents eroded or undeposited time — an almost incomprehensible interval during which entire mountain ranges rose and were worn flat.

John Wesley Powell's 1869 expedition through the canyon laid the groundwork for American stratigraphy.

concepts.title: Siccar Point — Hutton's Unconformity
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1788, James Hutton visited Siccar Point on the Scottish coast, where vertical Silurian shales (greywacke) are overlain by gently dipping Devonian red sandstone. The contact between them is an unconformity — a surface representing a gap in the record.

Hutton realised this implied an enormous sequence of events: the older shales were deposited, tilted to vertical by mountain building, eroded flat over vast time, then the younger sandstone was deposited on top. His companion John Playfair wrote that 'the mind seemed to grow giddy looking so far back into the abyss of time.'

This observation inspired Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism — present processes explain past events.

concepts.title: The K-Pg Boundary — A Global Timestamp
concepts.contentHtml:
The Cretaceous–Paleogene (K-Pg) boundary, 66 million years ago, is one of the most recognisable layers in the global rock record. It appears as a thin (<1 cm) clay layer enriched in iridium, shocked quartz, and microscopic glass spherules — signatures of a massive asteroid impact.

Luis and Walter Alvarez discovered the iridium anomaly at Gubbio, Italy in 1980. The same layer has since been found at hundreds of sites worldwide. It is a perfect event bed: deposited essentially simultaneously, globally, defining an instant in geological time.

Below the boundary: abundant non-avian dinosaur fossils. Above: none. The boundary marks the K-Pg mass extinction with millimetre precision.

title: Modern Stratigraphy and the Anthropocene
description: Correlating layers globally and reading our own impact in rock

concepts.title: Sequence Stratigraphy
concepts.contentHtml:
Sequence stratigraphy interprets sedimentary packages in terms of sea-level changes. When sea level rises, marine sediments advance onto land (transgression); when it falls, rivers cut down and erode (regression). These cycles create recognisable packages of strata bounded by unconformities.

Pioneered in the 1970s–80s using seismic reflection data from the oil industry, sequence stratigraphy revolutionised the prediction of where petroleum reservoir sands and sealing shales are located. It is now the standard framework for understanding large-scale sedimentary basins worldwide and for predicting future coastal change under sea-level rise.

concepts.title: Chemostratigraphy and Isotope Records
concepts.contentHtml:
Chemostratigraphy correlates rock layers using chemical signatures rather than fossils or physical appearance. Changes in the ratio of carbon, oxygen, or strontium isotopes in carbonates record global events — ocean acidification, temperature shifts, volcanic pulses.

The oxygen isotope record in deep-sea foraminifera shells provides a 50-million-year temperature history of the oceans — each foram shell is a thermometer for its era. Rapid isotope excursions mark dramatic events like the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM, 56 Ma), when the ocean warmed ~5 °C in tens of thousands of years — a geological precedent for rapid carbon-driven warming.

concepts.title: The Anthropocene — A New Stratigraphic Unit?
concepts.contentHtml:
Geologists are debating whether human activity has left a sufficiently distinct global signal in the rock record to define a new epoch: the Anthropocene.

Candidate markers include:
— A sharp rise in microplastics and artificial radionuclides (from nuclear tests) in lake and ocean sediments, starting ~1950.
— The global spread of fly ash from coal burning.
— A shift in carbon isotope ratios from fossil fuel burning.

The International Stratigraphic Commission debated the proposal for years and in 2024 formally voted against recognising it as an official epoch — but the concept has transformed how geologists think about human impact on Earth systems.
